10.1016_j.pmatsci.2026.101872: With their unmatched electrical-to-chemical conversion efficiency, solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) are increasingly recognized as a cornerstone technology for the green energy transition. Realizing this potential, however, critically depends on the durability of key stack components, most notably the metallic interconnects. Metallic interconnects in solid oxide electrolysis cells must withstand aggressive high-temperature, dual-atmosphere conditions. This review evaluates the current state of metallic interconnect materials for SOEC stacks, drawing on the more extensive Solid Oxide Fuel Cell (SOFC) literature while highlighting key differences. The analysis is structured around oxidation behavior on the oxygen and hydrogen/steam sides and dual-atmosphere effects, with emphasis on the interplay between chromia scale growth, chromium volatilization, and breakaway oxidation and their impact on interconnect lifetime and electrical performance. Key distinctions in SOEC operation including high steam content, reversed current polarity, and dual-atmosphere exposure are highlighted, revealing conditions where SOFC-based insights fail or require modification. The review evaluates alloy design and coating strategies and identifies critical knowledge gaps, particularly in low-temperature steam-side corrosion and dual-atmosphere degradation, outlining priorities for SOEC-specific material development
10.1038_s41467-026-72145-w: Radioactive organic wastewater management concerning metal source recovery and organic matter degradation conforms well to the notion of circular economy and environmental protection, but the concurrent conversion in an integrated process is challenging and has been rarely studied. Here, we introduce a high-performance photoelectrochemical system for uranyl extraction and the simultaneous degradation of co-existing urea to manage the treatment of uranyl-containing radioactive organic wastewater generated from the production of nuclear fuel for fourth-generation high-temperature gas-cooled reactor. Cost-efficient self-standing Ni-modified TiO 2 nanotube arrays (Ni/TiO 2 ) and β-cyclodextrin polymer (P-CDP@CC) were used as photoanode and cathode, respectively. Concurrent photoanodic urea degradation and cathodic uranyl reduction towards UO 2 from low-level radioactive organic wastewater demonstrated a uranyl extraction efficiency of 99.08% and the urea degradation efficiency of nearly 100% under a current density of 4.5 mA/cm 2 within 8 hours in a single-compartment electrolysis cell. This work provides an effective, environmentally benign approach to upcycle uranium resources and purify organic pollutants from complicated wastewater matrix.
